title: Three times, "read"
hookLine: the angel presses him and says read, three times, and then the first five verses (96:1–5; Bukhari)

lines: READ. I AM NOT A READER.
cards: Read. I am not a reader. That exchange happens once in the cave, then again, then a third time.

In between, the hadith says, the angel takes hold of him and presses him until he can hardly bear it. It's a strange, rough beginning: not a vision of light, but a grip, a word repeated, and a man saying he can't.
Today's word is about the repeating: three times.

teach.b: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. The angel came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave and said: read. He answered, in Arabic, ma ana bi-qari'.
The wording reads most naturally as a denial: I am not one who reads, I can't. Some scholars, pointing to other narrations worded differently, also hear a question: what shall I read?
Then the angel took hold of him and pressed him hard, released him, and said again: read. The same answer. A second pressing.
Read. The same answer. A third pressing.
And then the angel didn't ask. He recited. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot."
And a few lines on: "Teacheth man that which he knew not." The order matters. The command doesn't come with the ability attached.
He says he can't, three times, and the words come anyway, recited to him. He carries them home, his heart trembling, the hadith says.
Qur'an lessons still have something of that night's shape: a line heard, said back, heard again, until it stays.
And in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the one skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble, honored scribes, and the one who recites it with difficulty, struggling over it, gets a double reward.

how: Muslims memorize and learn the Qur'an by repetition, reciting a passage aloud to a teacher again and again until it is held by heart.

o: the nights he stayed in the cave each visit
the times a day the first Muslims prayed
the angel's read, and his I can't, three times

p: until he could hardly bear it

s: the angel recited the verses the first time he spoke
he said read three times, and only then recited surah 96.
ma ana bi-qari' can be read two ways
it reads as 'I am not a reader'; some, from other narrations, also hear 'what shall I read?'
a hadith gives extra reward to the one who struggles to recite
a double reward, in Sahih al-Bukhari.

games.q: you've said you can't, twice, and been pressed hard twice. the voice says read a third time. what happens?
o: you find you can read after all.
you say it again, and the words are given to you.
the angel leaves without a word.
games.why: he answered the same a third time, and then the angel recited: read, in the name of thy Lord. the words came anyway.

practice: Take one short passage that's hard for you, a verse, a poem, a paragraph, and read it three times, slowly: once without trying to understand it all, once listening for one word that catches, once letting it stay.
If you pray, you can use the line from today: read, in the name of thy Lord.

wordCard.voice: Three times. The angel said read, and the Prophet said I am not a reader, three times, before the first verses of surah ninety-six were given to him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: his answer in the cave, 'I am not a reader', or 'what shall I read?'

carryVoice: Your line: read, and read again. The one who struggles still gets a double reward. That's day seven hundred twenty-four.
